title: Michigan Primary Shocker: Progressive El-Sayed Clinches Senate Nomination
summary: Tuesday's primaries delivered a jolt to the political landscape. In Michigan, progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens, who had the backing of the party establishment. The race was a crucial test for the progressive movement's populist agenda—including Medicare for All—in a true swing state. El-Sayed's victory signals that a significant portion of Democratic voters are hungry for bold, systemic change. The stakes are high: Democrats need to win this seat to have a shot at controlling the Senate. But El-Sayed faces a formidable Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, in November. The general election promises to be a fierce battle. Progressives also celebrated a win in Michigan's only toss-up House district, where William Lawrence emerged as the nominee to challenge incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett. And in a stunning upset, Donavan McKinney unseated Rep. Shri Thanedar in the 13th Congressional District. However, the establishment struck back elsewhere. In Missouri, Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in a rematch. Bell was backed by the national party and pro-Israel groups, while Bush had support from democratic socialists and Sen. Bernie Sanders. The race highlighted deep divisions over U.S. policy toward Israel. Money played an outsized role. According to Open Secrets, outside groups poured a staggering $52 million into Michigan's Senate race by mid-July—second only to Texas in outside spending. El-Sayed sharply criticized the influence of AIPAC, a pro-Israel PAC that spent millions backing Stevens. His message resonated with voters frustrated by the role of big money in politics. On the Republican side, Trump's endorsement power remained potent. His picks won primaries in Washington, Kansas, and Michigan. In Washington's 4th District, Amanda McKinney beat 10 rivals for an open seat, though Trump-endorsed candidates have historically struggled in that conservative district. The results underscore a Democratic Party grappling with its identity, while Trump continues to tighten his grip on the GOP. As the general election approaches, these primaries offer a preview of the intense clashes to come.
why_it_matters: These primaries show that money and ideology are pulling the two major parties in opposite directions, which could affect everything from healthcare and immigration to foreign policy. Young people will inherit a political system shaped by these battles—whether it becomes more divided or whether new voices can change the direction of the country.

background_read: Primary elections are a uniquely American process: voters choose which candidate will represent their party in the November general election. They often reveal deep divisions within a party. The Open Secrets website tracks campaign finance and reported that outside groups—not the candidates themselves—spent $52 million on Michigan's Senate race by mid-July, second only to Texas.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as AIPAC, is one of the most influential lobbying groups in Washington. It backs candidates from both parties who support a strong U.S.-Israel relationship. Its super PAC spent millions to help Haley Stevens, a move some progressives criticized as interference in Democratic primaries.

Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, is a leading figure in the progressive movement and often uses the term 'democratic socialist.' He supported Abdul El-Sayed, showing the growing influence of his wing of the party. In Missouri, however, the establishment-backed Wesley Bell defeated Cori Bush, a fellow progressive, in a rematch that highlighted the ongoing struggle for the Democratic Party's identity.

Michigan is a classic swing state. In 2024 it voted for Donald Trump for president but also elected a Democrat to the Senate—proving it can swing either way. Control of the U.S. Senate is extremely close, and the Michigan seat is one of a handful that could tip the balance.

perspectives.description: El-Sayed's win and other progressive victories suggest that Democratic voters want bold, systemic changes like Medicare for All and less corporate influence. This energizes grassroots activists and could force the party to adopt a more ambitious agenda to turn out young and working-class voters in November.

The heavy spending by pro-Israel and other outside groups, together with establishment losses in some races, reveals a party deeply split on both policy and process. Critics argue that big money tilts the playing field and that internal fighting could weaken Democrats against Republicans, potentially handing the Senate to the GOP.

The results are a mix: progressives made gains in Michigan but lost in Missouri, showing no single faction has a clear grip on the party. The outsized role of outside spending—second only to Texas in this primary—points to a systemic trend where party primaries become national proxies for broader ideological fights, making candidates less accountable to local voters.

If El-Sayed wins in November, it could encourage more progressive candidates to run in swing states, possibly transforming the Senate in the long term. However, a loss might confirm the establishment's warning that such candidates can't win general elections, leading to a retreat. The tug-of-war over the party's identity, combined with Trump's continued dominance over the GOP, suggests that the 2026 midterms will be fiercely contested.
